candidates.title: Ring wants to put a drone in your house right as towns are kicking out Flock
candidates.full_text:
2026 is the year America started unplugging its surveillance cameras, and Ring chose that exact year to launch cameras that follow you around. Cities and counties have been dropping Flock Safety’s license plate readers at a record pace, with one anti-surveillance group counting roughly 90 cancellations in August alone. Into that mood rolls Ring Robotics, Amazon’s new lineup of security cameras that move on their own. There’s the Ring Drone Cam, a $249.99 drone that flies through your home, and the Ring Rover Cam, a $999.99 robot that patrols businesses after hours. Reading the room has never been Ring’s strong suit, but this is impressive even by its standards.

Ring has history with Flock, too. In October 2025, the two companies announced a deal to route police footage requests through Ring’s Community Requests feature. Four months later, Ring killed it after a Super Bowl ad about finding lost dogs creeped out a lot of viewers. Ring blamed the breakup on time and resources, which is the corporate version of saying you’ve been too busy to text back. Meanwhile, Flock kept making headlines for officers allegedly using its network to track ex-partners. A brand that nearly plugged into that system now wants its cameras flying up your stairs, and my answer is a polite no thanks.

The Drone Cam weighs 165 grams (0.36 pounds) and carries a 2K camera with a 148-degree field of view, plus two LEDs for night patrols. Setup involves carrying it through your house like an expensive newborn so it can sketch a floor plan, after which it flies preset routes or launches whenever a Ring sensor trips. Flights last somewhere between 5 and 10 minutes depending on whose numbers you trust, and every minute in the air costs roughly eight minutes on the dock. So if your back door sensor trips twice in an hour, the drone checks the first one and naps through the sequel. Lose Wi-Fi mid-flight and it simply lands wherever it happens to be, guarding the rug.

The Rover Cam is Amazon’s Astro robot with a security badge pinned on, shipping December 16. It rolls through shops, offices, and stockrooms on scheduled patrols, raising a periscope camera up to 4 feet (about 1.2 meters) to peer over shelves while streaming up to 4K video. Ring added a light tower that projects a blue circle onto the ceiling so you can find the thing, flipping to a spinning red light and a siren when something looks wrong. Both robots run on AI Pilot, Ring’s navigation system, which does most of its thinking in the cloud. Scheduled patrols require a Ring Protect subscription, and the drone still needs FCC authorization before it can actually ship on January 27, 2027.

Amazon sold Astro for Business to small companies in late 2023 for $2,349.99, plus a $60 monthly subscription to unlock patrol routes. About seven months later it shut the program down, and on September 25, 2024, every unit stopped working. Owners got refunds, a $300 credit, and a shipping label to recycle a robot that couldn’t even be converted into the home version. The Rover is cheaper, but it targets the exact shop owner Amazon already left holding a dead robot. Amazon never disclosed how many Astros it sold, and companies rarely keep the good numbers secret.

The drone’s biggest engineering win doubles as its biggest liability. Ring got it down to 165 grams by moving the brains to the cloud, which means a room-by-room map of your home lives on Amazon’s servers. The privacy features are genuine hardware, with a dock that covers the lens and propellers loud enough to announce every flight. They protect you from the drone, and they do nothing about who can request its footage later from a company that once handed police discounted doorbells and nearly plugged into Flock. Towns are pulling Flock cameras off their poles this year, and my bet is that Ring’s flying camera lasts about as long as Astro for Business did.

candidates.title: $1,100 off drops the Mammotion Luba 3 AWD 3000 to $1,999
candidates.full_text:
Mammotion’s flagship mower just took its biggest cut of the season. The Luba 3 AWD 3000 is $1,999 at Amazon, down from a $3,099 list price. That’s $1,100 off, a 35 percent cut, on the wire-free mower Mammotion rates for lawns up to three quarters of an acre.

This is the top of the Luba line, not a stripped variant built for a sale page. All-wheel drive, a 360-degree LiDAR turret, satellite positioning and dual AI cameras all ride on the same machine. The Amazon listing bundles the mower cleaning stand in the box, and an extra set of blades comes with it.

Mammotion Luba 3 AWD 3000 Robot Lawn Mower (Standard Version, 1.0″-2.7″) Tri-Fusion 360° LiDAR, NetRTK and dual-camera AI vision · All-wheel drive rated for 80% slopes · Covers up to 0.75 acre, 175 minutes per charge Price: $1,999 $3,099 (save $1,100, 35% off) at Amazon Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

Most wire-free mowers lean on a single positioning system and lose the plot under tree cover. The Luba 3 stacks three. A 360-degree LiDAR spins up top, NetRTK pulls satellite corrections down over the network, and dual cameras read the yard in front of the deck, so one system covers when another fades.

Mammotion quotes positioning accuracy at plus or minus 0.4 inches. There’s no base station to mount, level and run power to. You map the lawn in the app, and the mower works from that map, cutting the straight rows NetRTK positioning is built for. Setup is a mapping walk, not a construction project.

NetRTK corrections stay free for the life of the product. The built-in 4G connection is covered for the first three years, too. A 10-TOPS AI chip runs obstacle and pet detection on board, and the LiDAR sits under an armored alloy cover Mammotion rates at four times the durability of an exposed sensor. LiDAR and NetRTK keep their fix after dark, so a night mow runs on the same positioning as a noon one.

Plenty of robot mowers stall on a damp hillside. This one drives all four wheels and carries an 80 percent slope rating, 38.6 degrees. That covers the banks, swales and drainage grades that stop cheaper machines cold.

The chassis pairs high-strength aluminum with UV-resistant composites, and the whole mower weighs 41 pounds.

Light for its size. That weight counts on soft spring turf, where a heavier machine ruts the lawn it’s supposed to be grooming.

Underneath, two cutting discs spin a combined 15.7-inch width, each disc driven by its own 165-watt motor and carrying six blades. Blade speed runs up to 3,000 RPM, with a slower setting when quiet mowing beats fast mowing. Cut height adjusts from 1.0 to 2.7 inches on this Standard version, low enough for a tight finish on cool-season grass.

Runtime runs 175 minutes per charge, and Mammotion rates one charge at up to 0.42 acre of finished mowing. Across recharges, a day’s work covers the mower’s full 0.75-acre rating.

The pack refills in about two hours between runs, and a 210-watt fast charger ships in the box.

The bundled cleaning stand earns its keep at blade-swap time. It holds the mower up off the ground, discs reachable, no wrestling 41 pounds around the patio to get at the underside. The six-blade discs keep those swaps quick, and the spare blade set in the box covers the first one.

Multi-zone support runs to 50 mowing areas, with paths drawn between front and back yards so the mower commutes on its own.

Up to ten full lawn maps back up to the cloud. That suits anyone mowing a second property, or keeping a parent’s yard on the same account.

Partial remapping redraws one rough edge without scrapping the whole map, and edge fine-tuning cleans up curved beds and sharp corners. A wildlife mode slows or pauses night mowing around small animals. When the dock sits idle, EcoSleep drops it into a deep sleep that Mammotion says saves up to 100 kilowatt-hours a year.

The map stays editable after the first mow, too. Flexible editing lets you redraw a boundary after the landscapers move a bed, shift a zone line when a trampoline lands in the back corner, or split one big area into strips that mow on different days.

At $1,999, the AWD 3000 lands where a big, sloped or heavily shaded yard justifies the spend. Flat quarter-acre lots can run the smaller Luba 3 AWD 1500 for less. Anyone who needs a taller cut should price the High version of this same mower, which lifts the deck range to 4.0 inches and skips this discount entirely.

We’ve followed this line since the original Luba AWD 5000, which we reviewed hands-on back in 2023

candidates.title: This Tiny House Trades a Sleeping Loft for a Ground-Floor Bedroom
candidates.full_text:
A ladder still has a place inside the Cali 9.6, but climbing it isn’t part of going to bed. This tiny house by Australian builder Highlands Tiny Homes keeps its bedroom on the main floor, reserving the overhead crawl space for storage. It’s a practical distinction: the bed gets standing room, while less frequently needed belongings take the awkward space beneath the roof.

Measuring 9.6 meters long and 2.5 meters wide, approximately 31.5 by 8.2 feet, the Cali sits on a triple-axle trailer. Its pitched roof and pale exterior give it a cottage-like profile, with horizontal siding along the sides and vertical paneling at the end. Large sliding glass doors interrupt the narrow footprint, creating a broad opening beside the living area.

Inside, the timber-lined ceiling follows the roof pitch rather than flattening the room into a low rectangular box. Pale grooved walls, soft green cabinetry, and wood-look flooring establish a restrained palette, while black ceiling fans and brass-toned handles provide contrast. The manufacturer’s photographs show a compact sofa facing the kitchen peninsula, with the glazing running alongside the seating area rather than being confined to one end.

That peninsula is an important piece of planning. It provides a breakfast counter and preparation surface while marking the kitchen’s boundary without enclosing it. Drawers put storage beneath the worktop, making the divider useful on more than one level. Highlands lists faux stone benchtops, a two-burner gas cooktop, an under-counter four-in-one oven, and a ducted range hood among the standard inclusions.

The bathroom introduces the layout’s clearest compromise. Positioned between the living space and bedroom, it doubles as the connecting passage. A glass-enclosed shower occupies one side, with a vanity, cabinetry, and laundry appliance opposite. Patterned floor tiles give this narrow room a distinct character. Combining circulation and bathing space avoids allocating a separate hallway, but someone moving between the two main rooms must pass through the bathroom.

Beyond it, the bedroom accommodates a double bed beneath the pitched timber ceiling. Built-in bedside drawers and a wall-spanning arrangement of cupboards and open shelves concentrate storage around the headboard. Wall-mounted reading lights leave the small bedside surfaces free. The bedroom also has its own exterior glass doors, providing a separate way outside. This is a dedicated sleeping room, with no nightly furniture conversion required.

The Cali 9.6 is listed from US$100,000, including GST. Its strongest selling point is giving a permanent bedroom priority within a narrow plan. The walk-through bathroom is the price of that arrangement, and the detail prospective owners should consider as carefully as the appealing timber ceiling.
